sections.h2: Where Dallas County property records are kept
sections.html:
For land records in Dallas County, go to the Recording Division of the County Clerk. It works from the Records Building, 500 Elm Street, Suite 2100, Dallas, TX 75202, and holds the Official Public Records: deeds, mortgages, releases and more.

The office records roughly 400,000 documents a year: deeds, liens against a property, transfers between owners, probate papers that touch land, and the release of lien filed once a mortgage is paid off. Its purpose is to show the public who holds a financial interest in a parcel.

  • Phone: (214) 653-7099
  • Hours: weekdays, opening at 8:00 a.m. and closing at 4:30 p.m., with court-approved holidays off
  • Mail: Dallas County Clerk's Office, Recording Division, 500 Elm Street, STE 2100, Dallas, Texas 75202
  • Questions the FAQ page does not answer: recording@dallascounty.org

A seller will touch this office through the title company, since the title search and the filing of the new deed both run through these records. Start at the Recording Division page.

Begin with the clerk's Online Public Record Search, which returns non-certified images. Pay for a certified copy only if a lender, court or title company demands it. The free search and the certified service are two different things.

Certified electronic copies of Official Public Record documents are sold on the clerk's website around the clock. Each carries the clerk's digital signature and tamper-proof encryption, so a buyer's lender can accept it without a paper original. Counter and mail requests for real property copies run $1.00 a page, and a certified copy adds $5.00 for each document.

Plat copies are priced separately: $6.00 per page for the large 18 by 24 size and $1.00 per page for 8.5 by 11, with the same $5.00 certification fee per plat. The clerk holds only plats filed with that office, so a subdivision map recorded elsewhere will not be there.

Recorded deeds sometimes carry a Social Security number, driver's license number, date of birth or bank account number. Under House Bill 2061, that information may be eligible for redaction. The owner files a Redaction Request Form by mail or in person. Any other change to a recorded document needs a later filing, so ask a lawyer whether a correction document or a fresh deed is the right fix.

A standard document costs $25.00 on page one and $4.00 on each page after. Of the $25.00, $5.00 pays for recording, $10.00 for records preservation and $10.00 for archiving.

Writing on the back of the last sheet is billed as a full $4.00 page, so a signature block that spills onto a reverse side costs the same as a new page. A few specialty documents have their own fees, and some filings, such as child support liens and military discharge papers, carry no filing fee.

Payment rules are strict. Acceptable payment is cash, money order, cashier's check or business check, payable to the Dallas County Clerk. It does not accept personal checks. Cards work only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit or $2.85 on pin debit. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with mailed filings if you want the stamped copy back.

sections.h2: What the clerk requires before recording a deed
sections.html:
The deed has to be signed and properly acknowledged, and a photo ID is required for documents that convey property from one person to another. House Bill 1195 put that rule in place on July 1, 2023.

  • Acknowledgment. A notary, another authorized officer or two subscribing witnesses must attest to the signature.
  • Court-ordered papers. Anything that originates in a lawsuit has to arrive as a certified copy, authenticated by the court or its clerk.
  • Grantee address. Leave off the buyer's mailing address and a $25 charge may follow.
  • Notary on site. A notary sits on the fourth floor in the Treasurer's office from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. daily for $10, cash only.
  • Electronic filing. Local Government Code Sec. 195.003 limits e-recording to attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally approved lenders, state-regulated lenders, title insurers and agents, and state agencies.

An individual who is not on that list files on paper at the Elm Street counter or by mail, or lets the title company submit the deed electronically after closing.

sections.h2: Dallas County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Dallas County had an estimated 2,661,397 residents in July 2025, up 1.9 percent from the 2020 base, across 873.06 square miles and 1,099,775 housing units. The owner-occupied rate is 50.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, so roughly half of households rent. With a tenant in the house, the title company will want the lease.

The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $303,000. Median gross rent is $1,565. Builders pulled 12,691 permits in 2025. Median monthly owner costs run $2,166 with a mortgage and $793 without one. A house with no mortgage is simpler to transfer, because there is no lender payoff and no release of lien to track down.

sections.h2: Record problems that slow a sale
sections.html:
Unreleased liens, unfiled estate paperwork and tax debts cause most delays, and all of them show up in the clerk's records. A title company runs the search before closing and flags what it finds.

  • Old mortgages. A paid-off loan should have a recorded release of lien. If none was filed, the lender has to be contacted to issue one.
  • Tax liens. State and federal tax lien notices are filed with the clerk, and the clerk lists fixed fees for both and for their releases.
  • Foreclosure notices. Notices of sale are posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk, usually 21 or more days before the sale.
  • Estates without a clean chain. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the clerk, but no buyer or lender has to accept it. Probate or a court order may be safer.
  • Hospital and child support liens. Both have to be cleared if they attach to the property.

If any of these turn up, ask the title company which instrument cures the problem and who files it.

The county's claim for each year's tax begins January 1 and rests on whoever holds title that day. A November sale leaves that claim in place, so the closing statement has to say who pays it.

Statements arrive near October 1. February 1 is when a balance goes delinquent, adding six percent penalty and one percent interest, and the penalty climbs a point a month through July 1. Installments are open to owners over 65 or disabled. Before closing, call the Dallas County tax office for the balance and ask the appraisal district whether a homestead exemption is on file. A buyer may be able to claim an unused exemption for the remainder of the year.

faqs.q: What is the first-page charge for a deed at the Dallas County Clerk?
faqs.a: The first page is $25.00 and every extra page is $4.00. Of the first-page fee, $5.00 is for recording and $10.00 each is for records preservation and archiving. Anything printed on a page's back is billed as a full page.

faqs.q: Can I pay Dallas County recording fees with a personal check?
faqs.a: No. The clerk accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and business checks payable to the Dallas County Clerk. Cards are taken only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit cards or $2.85 on pin debit.

faqs.q: Are the documents in the online public record search certified?
faqs.a: No. Online search results are non-certified. Electronic certified copies carry the clerk's digital signature and are sold through a separate service. Paper certified copies are $1.00 a page plus $5.00 a document.

faqs.q: Can I e-record my own deed in Dallas County?
faqs.a: Usually not. Electronic recording is limited to attorneys, banks, certain lenders, title companies and state agencies. An individual owner normally files on paper at 500 Elm Street or has a title company file the deed.

faqs.q: How do I remove a Social Security number from a recorded document?
faqs.a: File a Redaction Request Form with the clerk, by mail or in person. House Bill 2061 makes personal data such as Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, dates of birth and account numbers eligible for redaction.
